questions.title: Releasing a patient's records without consent
questions.question: A man asked the psychiatrist of his 25-year-old brother to release his brother's records. For which of the following actions can the patient sue the psychiatrist?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abandonment is the unilateral ending of a treatment relationship without notice or handover; disclosing records is not abandonment.
explanations.B: Correct. Releasing a competent adult patient's records to his brother without the patient's consent is a breach of confidentiality, for which the patient can sue. The 25-year-old is a competent adult whose information may not be disclosed to a relative without his authorisation. The wrong here is unauthorised disclosure, not a failure of skill or care.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Incompetence is a lack of the expected knowledge or skill; improperly disclosing information is a confidentiality breach, not a competence issue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Negligence is a failure to meet the standard of care that causes harm; unauthorised disclosure of records is specifically a breach of confidentiality.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise unauthorised release of a competent patient's records as a breach of confidentiality.

questions.title: Guiding principle of the Hippocratic Oath
questions.question: According to the Hippocratic Oath, one of the following four principles might be regarded as a "guiding principle".

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy — respect for the patient's self-determination — is a modern bioethical principle emphasised long after the Oath, not its guiding commitment.
explanations.B: Correct. The guiding principle of the Hippocratic Oath is beneficence: the physician's positive commitment to act for the benefit of the sick and to use treatment to help the patient. The Oath is framed around doing good for the patient, which is beneficence. This overarching duty to benefit the patient is what marks it out from the other listed principles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Justice — fair distribution of benefits and burdens — is a principle of modern bioethics, not the guiding theme of the Oath.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Non-maleficence ("first do no harm") is closely associated with Hippocratic teaching, but the guiding principle keyed here is the positive duty of beneficence to benefit the patient.

questions.learning_objective: State that beneficence is regarded as the guiding principle of the Hippocratic Oath.

questions.title: Ethical principle behind first-come-first-managed triage
questions.question: After a bus accident, 12 patients were admitted to the emergency room. The doctor decided to treat the patients according to the rule of "first come, first managed". Here the doctor applied which basic ethical principle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abandonment is a failure of duty, not an ethical principle; it does not describe a fair allocation rule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence is acting for the patient's good; the specific issue here is how to allocate care fairly among many patients, which is justice.
explanations.C: Correct. Treating patients by a neutral "first come, first managed" rule applies the principle of justice — the fair and impartial distribution of a limited resource (the doctor's time) among competing patients. Justice governs how benefits and burdens are shared out, which is exactly what a queue rule does. That is why this scenario illustrates justice rather than beneficence or non-maleficence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Non-maleficence is the duty to avoid harm; it does not describe the fair-allocation rule the doctor is using.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise fair allocation of care (first-come-first-managed) as an application of justice.

questions.title: Definition of an ethical dilemma
questions.question: A conflict between two moral principles is defined as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Assault is causing another person to fear imminent unlawful force; it is not a conflict between moral principles.
explanations.B: Correct. A conflict between two moral principles is defined as an (ethical) dilemma: a situation in which two valid moral principles point to incompatible courses of action, so honouring one means breaching the other. The decision-maker must weigh the competing principles because both cannot be fully satisfied. This tension between valid principles is precisely what a dilemma denotes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Indecency refers to offensive or obscene conduct, not a clash of moral principles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Negligence is a failure to meet the standard of care causing harm, not a conflict between two moral principles.

questions.learning_objective: Define an ethical dilemma as a conflict between two moral principles.
